standfirst: Two military policemen chase deserters, one case per episode, and the question is always why the man ran rather than where he went. The reason it lands harder than its premise suggests: none of it is exaggerated. Several of the incidents are drawn from real cases, and the accuracy is the whole point. It is also funnier than you expect, which is deliberate and which the show never lets undercut the subject. Six episodes, and it is a lot to take.

picks.why: The obvious pairing, and it goes deeper than tone. Shared composer, overlapping cast, and the same insistence that bullying is a physical injury with a chain of command behind it rather than a character-building phase. Eight episodes, no filler, no romance, the same cold blue palette and the same ending register. Difference: a school rather than a barracks, and one protagonist rather than a duo, so you lose the friendship that makes D.P. survivable.

The same structure aimed at a different institution: a case per episode, no romance, and a system that fails predictably while individual people try anyway. Same refusal to hand you a villain to blame instead of a process. Difference: a courtroom rather than a manhunt, and no comedy at all. There is no Ho-yeol here to break the tension, and you feel the absence.

For the thing D.P. does best, which is reconstructing a person from what they left behind. Ten episodes of trauma cleaners piecing together lives nobody attended to, with the same quiet fury about people who were failed by everyone around them. Difference: grief rather than violence, and it is gentle. It will make you cry rather than make you angry.

The same two-young-men-against-the-system dynamic, moved onto a loan shark's payroll, and the comparison holds. Same age, same era of conscription-adjacent masculinity, same central friendship carrying the show. Difference: it is an action series with a villain to punch. D.P.'s whole point is that there is nobody to punch.

The other great Korean drama about a closed institution with a hierarchy that decides everything. Same interest in how men behave when rank is the only currency, and the same trick of getting real tenderness out of comedy. Difference: it is a comfort watch. Nobody is destroyed, and the institution is treated as absurd rather than as dangerous.

If what stayed with you was the cycle of abuse and how ordinary the people maintaining it are. A community that would rather not know, seniors protecting seniors, and sixteen episodes of moral discomfort. Difference: it is a serial-killer mystery with a puzzle to solve. D.P. has no mystery. You know exactly what happened and who allowed it.

against.title: Squid Game
against.why: The reflex pick after any bleak Korean Netflix show. It is a survival allegory with rules, costumes and a game structure, and its cruelty is designed. D.P. is a procedural about paperwork, hazing and a chain of command. Shared distributor, nothing else.

against.title: The Glory
against.why: Suggested for the bullying overlap, and it is the wrong shape. The Glory offers eighteen years of preparation and then catharsis. D.P.'s entire argument is that there is no catharsis available, only the next case. Watch one expecting the other and you will come away frustrated.

against.title: Duty After School
against.why: Also Korean, also military, also about young men handed weapons, and that is where it ends. It is a science-fiction horror series about an alien threat. The uniform is the only thing the two shows share.
